**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat al-Raḥmān, verses 1–13:**

[p. 158] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsīr of Sūrat al-Raḥmān (the exegesis of the chapter)**

It is a Meccan surah according to the majority of the Companions and the Successors. Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Nuʿaym, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, Kurayb, and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is Madinan, revealed when Suhayl ibn ʿAmr and others refused to have "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" written in the treaty. The first view is more sound. It was revealed when the Quraysh in Mecca said: ﴿And what is the Most Gracious? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqān: 60]. In the biographical literature (al-sīrah) it is related that Ibn Masʿūd recited it aloud in the mosque, until the gatherings of the Quraysh rose against him and beat him. This was before the Hijrah.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿The Most Gracious﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ ﴿created man﴾ ﴿taught him expression﴾ ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning﴾ ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾ ﴿and the sky He raised, and He set the balance﴾ ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ ﴿and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient﴾ ﴿and the earth He laid out for the creatures﴾ ﴿therein is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths﴾ ﴿and grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾

"Al-Raḥmān" is an intensive form (bināʾ mubālaghah) derived from mercy (al-raḥmah). It is a name that Allah, exalted is He, is specifically described by. Ibn Fawrak related from a group that they treat "al-Raḥmān" as a complete verse, as if the implied meaning is "The Most Gracious is our Lord," and al-Rummānī said this, and that the implied meaning is "Allah, the Most Gracious." The majority, however, hold that the verse is "The Most Gracious taught the Qur'an," so it is part of a verse.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is an enumeration of a blessing, meaning: He bestowed it upon them and taught it to people, and He singled out those who memorise it and understand it with merit. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of you is the one who learns the Qur'an and teaches it." Among the evidence that the Qur'an is not created is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the Qur'an in His Book in fifty-four places, none of which uses the word "creation" explicitly or alludes to it. He mentioned man (al-insān) in a third of that, in eighteen places, all of which state his creation explicitly. The two are mentioned together in this surah in this manner.

"Al-Insān" here is the generic noun (ism al-jins), related by al-Zahrāwī and others. "Al-bayān" means speech, understanding, and clear expression through utterance. This was said by Ibn Zayd and the majority, and it is this that distinguishes man from the rest of the animals. Qatādah said: it is the clarification of the lawful and the unlawful and the legal rulings, and this is a part of the general clarification. Qatādah also said: "al-insān" is Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Kaysān said: "al-insān" is Muhammad ﷺ. This specification has no evidence. All knowable things are included in the expression that man was taught. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, said: from that expression, and within it is the lesson of the sun and the moon being by a reckoning. He omitted all of this, and "al-shams" (the sun) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and this is the beginning of the enumeration of blessings.

People differed regarding His saying ﴿bi-ḥusbān﴾ ("by a reckoning"). Makkī and al-Zahrāwī related from Qatādah that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of ḥisāb (calculation), like ghufrān (forgiveness) and ṭughyān (transgression) in pattern. Abū ʿUbaydah Maʿmar said: for them, in their rising, setting, and traversing of the mansions (burūj) and other things, there are calculations. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Mālik, and Qatādah. Ibn Zayd said: were it not for the night and the day, no one would know how to calculate anything of the measures of time. Mujāhid said: al-ḥusbān is the revolving orb, likened to the ḥusbān of the millstone, which is the rotating piece of wood by whose turning the grinding stone turns.

His saying ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, and Sufyān said: [p. 160] "al-najm" is the plant that has no stem, and it is called najm because it "najama," that is, it appeared and rose up. It is fitting for the tree to be compared to it. Mujāhid, Qatādah, and al-Ḥasan said: "al-najm" is the generic noun for the stars of the sky, and the relation it has to the sky is the same as that of the tree to the earth, because both are apparent. The tree (al-shajar) is so named from ishtijār (interlacing) of its branches, which is their intertwining. People differed about this prostration. Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said: for the star it is by its setting and the like, and for the tree it is by its shadow and its turning. Likewise, for the star on the other view. Mujāhid also said, in substance, that prostration in all of this is figurative, meaning submission and humbling oneself and the like. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴾ ................. you see the hills prostrating to the hooves [of the horses]

He, exalted is He, said "yasjudān" (they prostrate), which is a dual, while the subject is two things; this is because He observed the wording, since the word (najm) is a singular noun that denotes a category. This is like the saying of the poet:

﴾ Has it not grieved you that the ropes of my people and of your people have been severed in separation?

The majority recited ﴿and the sky He raised﴾ in the accusative (naṣb), coordinating it with the minor clause "yasjudān," since this is a clause made of verb and agent, and this one is likewise. Abū al-Samāl recited it in the nominative, coordinating it with the major clause, which is His saying ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, since that clause is of subject and predicate, and the other is likewise. In the Muṣḥaf of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "wa-khafaḍa al-mīzān" (and He lowered the balance). The meaning of "waḍaʿa" is that He established and affirmed. "Al-mīzān" means justice, according to al-Ṭabarī, Mujāhid, and most people. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Qatādah said: it is the known balance (scale), which is a part of the balance by which justice is expressed. It appears to me that His saying ﴿and He set the balance﴾ means justice, while His saying ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾, His saying ﴿and establish the weight with justice﴾, and His saying ﴿and do not make the balance deficient﴾ mean the known balance. Everything that has been said is plausible and admissible.

His saying ﴿ألّا تطغوا﴾ ("that you not transgress") is a prohibition against deliberate transgression in the balance. As for what human beings cannot avoid in weighing exactly, that is waived for people. "Allā" is taken as "li-allā" (in order that not), or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi). "Taṭghaw" is in the subjunctive (manṣūb). It is possible that "an" is explanatory, in which case "taṭghaw" is in the jussive by the prohibition. In the Muṣḥaf of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "lā taṭghaw" without "an." Most people recited ﴿وَلَا تُخْسِرُوا﴾ from akhsara, meaning he diminished and corrupted. Bilāl ibn Abī Burdah recited "wa-tukhsirū" with a fatḥah on the taʾ and a kasrah on the sīn, from khasira. It is said that khasira means nāqaṣa and afsada (diminished and corrupted), like jabara and ajbara. Bilāl also recited, as related from him by Ibn Jinnī: "takhsarū," with a fatḥah on the taʾ and the sīn, from khasira with a kasrah on the sīn.

People differed about "al-anām." Ibn ʿAbbās, in one of the reports from him, said: they are the children of Adam alone. al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: they are the two weighty species, jinn and humankind. Ibn ʿAbbās also, along with Qatādah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Shaʿbī, said: they are all living animals. "Al-akmām" (sheaths) exist in the palm in both places: the entire branches of the palm are in sheaths of its fibre, and the palm's spathe (ṭalʿ) is in a sheath on one side. Qatādah said: the sheaths of the palm trees are their necks (riqāb).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Every "kimm" (covering) of plants is whatever wraps around something and covers it. From this come the sheaths of the flower, and from it the sleeve of a garment (kumm al-thawb) is so named.

[p. 162] ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾. "Al-ḥabb dhū al-ʿaṣf" is wheat, barley, and what is similar to them of grains that have ears and branching leaves on their stalks. The ʿaṣīfah is what dries of these. From this is the saying of ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbadah:

﴾ They are watered in channels whose ʿaṣīfah have inclined, and its troughs are full of the fresh water.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-ʿaṣf" is chaff (tibn). The Arabs say: "We went out to ta'aṣṣaf," that is, they gather the stalk of the crop. Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū al-Barhasim recited "wa-al-ḥabba" in the accusative, coordinating it with "al-arḍa": "dhā al-ʿaṣfi wa-al-raḥyāni"; except that Abū al-Barhasim lowered the nūn. They differed about "al-rayḥān." Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: its meaning is provision (rizq). From this is the saying of the poet, al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

﴾ The peace of God and His provision, and His Garden, and a sky pouring abundant rain.

al-Ḥasan said: it is "your rayḥān," this (i.e., this familiar plant). Ibn Jubayr said: it is whatever stands upon a stalk. Ibn Zayd and Qatādah said: al-rayḥān is every fragrant plant with a pleasant smell, and in this kind there is great blessing: from it are flowers, aloe, medicinal herbs, and other things. al-Farrāʾ said: al-ʿaṣf is what is eaten, and al-rayḥān is whatever is not eaten. Most people recited: "wa-al-ḥabbu dhū al-ʿaṣfi wa-al-rayḥāni." [p. 163] This reading, in meaning, is like the first, and in grammatical construction it is well coordinated, being coordinated with "fākihah" (fruit). Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn Muḥaysin recited "wa-al-ḥabbu" in the nominative, "dhū al-ʿaṣfi wa-al-rayḥāni" with "al-rayḥāni" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-ʿaṣf," as if "al-ḥabb" has them both, on the basis that "al-ʿaṣf" includes the leaves and everything that is crushed by the hand and the wind, and this is the provision of the beasts, while "al-rayḥān" includes the grain, which is the provision of humankind. On this reading, "al-rayḥān" does not include the fragrant plants except with a stretch. "Rayḥān" is from the roots with waw. Abū ʿAlī said: either rayḥān is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun, or it is a verbal noun on the pattern fiʿlān, like al-liyyān and what is similar to it, whose original is rawḥān, and the waw was changed to yā, as they changed yā to waw in "ashāwī." Or it is a verbal noun of an anomalous defective root, as with kaynūnah and baynūnah, so its original is rayawḥān; the waw was changed to yā and the yā was assimilated into yā, so it came out as rayḥān, which was lightened, as they said: mayt and mayyit, hayn and hayyin.

"Al-ālāʾ" are the blessings. Its singular is ilan, like miʿan and ulan like naqan; Abū ʿUbaydah related these two. And alyun, like amnin; and ilyun, like ḥiṣnin; al-Zahrāwī related these two. The pronoun in His saying ﴿rabbukumā﴾ ("your two Lords") refers to jinn and humankind. This was permissible even though they were not explicitly mentioned, on one of two grounds: either they were mentioned in His saying ﴿lil-anām﴾ (for the creatures), as has preceded, since it is meant as the two weighty species; or their affair is explained in His saying ﴿created man﴾ and ﴿and created the jinn﴾, so it was permissible to put them forward in the pronoun by way of latitude (ittisāʿ). al-Ṭabarī said: it is possible to say this is of the type of ﴿throw into Gehenna﴾ and "O boy, strike his neck." [p. 164] Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: the address is to one who understands, because the address of the entire Qur'an is to humankind and jinn. And it is related that when the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse, his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were silent. He ﷺ said: "The response of the jinn is better than your silence; when I recited it to the jinn, they said: We do not deny any of the blessings of our Lord."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrat al-Raḥmān, verses 1–13:**

[p. 158] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsīr of Sūrat al-Raḥmān (the exegesis of the chapter)**

It is a Meccan surah according to the majority of the Companions and the Successors. Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Nuʿaym, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, Kurayb, and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is Madinan, revealed when Suhayl ibn ʿAmr and others refused to have "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" written in the treaty. The first view is more sound. It was revealed when the Quraysh in Mecca said: ﴿And what is the Most Gracious? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqān: 60]. In the biographical literature (al-sīrah) it is related that Ibn Masʿūd recited it aloud in the mosque, until the gatherings of the Quraysh rose against him and beat him. This was before the Hijrah.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿The Most Gracious﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ ﴿created man﴾ ﴿taught him expression﴾ ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning﴾ ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾ ﴿and the sky He raised, and He set the balance﴾ ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ ﴿and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient﴾ ﴿and the earth He laid out for the creatures﴾ ﴿therein is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths﴾ ﴿and grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾

"Al-Raḥmān" is an intensive form (bināʾ mubālaghah) derived from mercy (al-raḥmah). It is a name that Allah, exalted is He, is specifically described by. Ibn Fawrak related from a group that they treat "al-Raḥmān" as a complete verse, as if the implied meaning is "The Most Gracious is our Lord," and al-Rummānī said this, and that the implied meaning is "Allah, the Most Gracious." The majority, however, hold that the verse is "The Most Gracious taught the Qur'an," so it is part of a verse.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is an enumeration of a blessing, meaning: He bestowed it upon them and taught it to people, and He singled out those who memorise it and understand it with merit. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of you is the one who learns the Qur'an and teaches it." Among the evidence that the Qur'an is not created is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the Qur'an in His Book in fifty-four places, none of which uses the word "creation" explicitly or alludes to it. He mentioned man (al-insān) in a third of that, in eighteen places, all of which state his creation explicitly. The two are mentioned together in this surah in this manner.

"Al-Insān" here is the generic noun (ism al-jins), related by al-Zahrāwī and others. "Al-bayān" means speech, understanding, and clear expression through utterance. This was said by Ibn Zayd and the majority, and it is this that distinguishes man from the rest of the animals. Qatādah said: it is the clarification of the lawful and the unlawful and the legal rulings, and this is a part of the general clarification. Qatādah also said: "al-insān" is Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Kaysān said: "al-insān" is Muhammad ﷺ. This specification has no evidence. All knowable things are included in the expression that man was taught. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, said: from that expression, and within it is the lesson of the sun and the moon being by a reckoning. He omitted all of this, and "al-shams" (the sun) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and this is the beginning of the enumeration of blessings.

People differed regarding His saying ﴿bi-ḥusbān﴾ ("by a reckoning"). Makkī and al-Zahrāwī related from Qatādah that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of ḥisāb (calculation), like ghufrān (forgiveness) and ṭughyān (transgression) in pattern. Abū ʿUbaydah Maʿmar said: for them, in their rising, setting, and traversing of the mansions (burūj) and other things, there are calculations. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Mālik, and Qatādah. Ibn Zayd said: were it not for the night and the day, no one would know how to calculate anything of the measures of time. Mujāhid said: al-ḥusbān is the revolving orb, likened to the ḥusbān of the millstone, which is the rotating piece of wood by whose turning the grinding stone turns.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 55, verses 14–18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾ ﴿and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾

Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: "al-Insan" refers to Adam, peace be upon him. Others said that it denotes the generic noun, and this is acceptable because their father was created from clay (salsal). People differed over the derivation of "salsal." Makki, as he related it, and al-Naqqash said: it comes from "salla al-lahm wa ghayruhu" (meat and other things became putrid) when they rot, so it refers to black mud (hama'a). Al-Tabari and the majority of the exegetes said: it derives from "salla" when it makes a sound (sawwata), and this refers to clay because of its purity and quality. So it refers to the good clay that was in Adam's dust, peace be upon him. That is because God, blessed and exalted, created him from good clay, foul clay, and clay of various colors; at one time He mentioned this in his creation, and at another time that. Everything in the Qur'an on this subject consists of attributes that recur regarding the dust from which he was created. "Al-Fakhkhar" is good clay when water touches it, so that it "fakhara," i.e., swelled and grew large.

"Al-Jann" is a generic noun, like "al-jinna." "Al-marij" is the agitated flame of fire. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is the best of fire, mixed with various colors. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "How will you be when you are among a worthless remnant of people, whose covenants and trusts have become confused?"

He repeated His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ as emphasis and as an alert to souls and a stirring of them. This is a well-known method of eloquence, and it occurs in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, in several places, in the Hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in the speech of the Arabs. A group, among them Ibn Qutayba and others, held that this repetition is only because the blessings mentioned differ, so with each one he repeated the reproach. This view is the best. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: the repetition serves to drive away heedlessness and to emphasize.

He, the Exalted, singled out the mention of the two easts and the two wests for honor in attributing the Lord to them, because of their greatness among created things, and because they are the two extremes of a great sign and lesson, which is the sun and its movement. al-Naqqash related that "the two easts" are the rising points of the sun and the moon, and "the two wests" likewise, with the lessons contained in that. All of these are valid. Whenever "al-mashriq" and "al-maghrib" are mentioned, they refer to the two directions in their entirety. Whenever "al-mashariq" and "al-maghareb" (plural) are mentioned, they refer to the rising and setting points of each day. Whenever "al-mashriqan" and "al-maghribani" (dual) are mentioned, they refer to the two extremes of the rising and setting points, because mentioning the two extremes of a thing is a mention of all of it. Mujahid said: it is the rising point of summer and its setting point, and the rising point of winter and its setting point.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 55, verse 19–28:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He released the two seas, meeting one another﴾ ﴿Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿And His are the ships, sailing high on the sea like mountains﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ ﴿And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

(p-166) "Maraja al-bahrayn" means: He let them flow freely, without one being separated from the other. From it comes "marajat al-dabbah" (the animal grazed freely), and from it "al-amr al-marij," meaning a confused matter from which nothing has been distinguished. And from it (is) ﴿from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. People differed concerning "al-bahrayn." Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. Al-Hasan also said: the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea) and the Sea of Yemen and the Sea of Sham. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: a sea in the sky and a sea on the earth. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: it is the rain of the sky, which he named a sea, and the sea of the earth. The apparent meaning in my view is that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿He released the two seas﴾, intends by them the two kinds of water, the sweet and the salty; that is, He mixed them on the earth and released them intermingled in their placement on the earth, close to one another. The lesson in this interpretation is luminous. Mundhir ibn Sa'id recited:

Mixed waters, in which the sweet does not dominate the salt, pure, nor does the salt become sweet.

As for the saying of the Exalted, "yaltaqiyan" (meeting), according to the first two interpretations its meaning is: they are prepared for meeting, and it is due that they would meet were it not for the barrier. According to the third view, they meet once every year. Whoever holds that it is a sea that gathers in the sky is stating a weak view; meeting is directed in it, and in the fourth view, toward the falling of rain, and in the fifth view, toward the rivers entering the sea and the springs near the sea.

And "al-barzakh" is the barrier in everything. In some of these views it is the bodies of the earth, as Qatadah said; in some it is power. Al-barzakh also refers to the period between this world and the Hereafter for the dead, since it is a barrier. Some people said: the water of rivers does not mix with salt water, but remains in its own essence within it. This requires evidence or a sound hadith; otherwise direct observation does not necessitate it. Al-Tha'labi mentioned in "maraj al-bahrayn" enigmas and esoteric sayings to which one should not give any attention.

People differed concerning the saying of the Exalted, "la yabghiyan" (they do not transgress). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: its meaning is: neither of them transgresses against the other. Qatadah and al-Hasan also said: they do not transgress against people and inhabited places. These two views take the word from "al-baghy" (transgression). Some interpreters said: it is from your saying "baghy" when one seeks. Its meaning then is: they do not seek any state other than their two states in which they were created and subjected for them. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "al-lu'lu'" is the large pearls and "al-marjan" is their small ones. (p-167) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, also said, as did Murrah al-Hamdani, the reverse of this. The description of smallness is the correct one for pearls. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: "al-marjan" is a red stone; this is the correct view for coral. "Al-lu'lu'" is a rare word pattern, of which no more than five are preserved in the speech of the Arabs: al-lu'lu', al-ju'ju', al-du'du', al-yu'yu' (which is a bird), and al-bu'bu', which is the original.

People differed concerning the saying of the Exalted, "minhuma" (from them). Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said in the book "al-Hujjah": some people claimed that pearls and coral do emerge from salt water and from sweet water. People refuted the poet in his saying:

He brought you whatever you wish of a lutmiyyah (a fine cloth), upon whose face the waters of the Euphrates surge.

(p-168) Most of the interpreters said: these things only emerge from the salt water in the places where rivers and sweet waters fall into it; therefore the Exalted said "minhuma." This is well known among divers. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: these things form in the sea through the falling of rain, because the oyster and others open their shells to the rain; therefore the Exalted said "minhuma." Abu 'Ubaydah said, in substance: the emergence of these things is only from the salt water, but the Exalted said "minhuma" figuratively, as the poet said:

.............. wearing a sword and a spear

And as another said:

.............. I fed them straw and cold water

(p-169) Since they are both one kind, the emergence of these things is indeed from both, even though in detail they belong specifically to one of them. This is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ [Nuh: 15] ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], whereas it is only in one of them, which is the nearest heaven to the earth. Al-Rummani said: the sweet water within them is like the pollen to the salt, so it is as one says: the child comes out of the male and the female. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the people of Madinah read "yakhruju" with a dammah on the ya' and a fathah on the ra', with "al-lu'lu'" in the nominative. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yakhraju" with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the ra', in the active form of the verb; this is also the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn al-Ju'fi from him, read "yukhriju" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the ra', attributing it to Allah the Exalted, that is, by His enabling and power, with "al-lu'lu'" in the accusative; he also transmitted it with a nun, dammah, and a kasrah on the ra'.

"Al-jawari" is the plural of "jariyah," and it means the ships. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read "al-jawariya" with the ya' affirmed; Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with the ya' deleted. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-munsha'at" with a fathah on the shin, meaning that Allah the Exalted or people brought them into being. Hamzah and Abu Bakr (with a variant transmitted from him) read "al-munshi'at" with a kasrah on the shin, meaning that they themselves produce the movement, advancing and retreating. "Al-a'lam" are the mountains and whatever is like them of hills and mounds. Mujahid said: whatever has a sail is among the munsha'at, and whatever has no sail raised for it is not among the munsha'at.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of the Exalted, "kal-a'lam" (like mountains), is what requires this distinction. As for the word "al-munsha'at," it includes the large and the small.

The pronoun in the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾, refers to the earth. Allah the Exalted referred to it by a pronoun without a prior mention of it (p-170) because the meaning is clear, as He said: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], and other evidences of this kind. The indication by "perishing" applies to all existing things upon the earth, of animals and others, so the expression for those who reason prevailed, and therefore He said "man" (whoever).

"Al-wajh" (the Face) is an expression for the Essence, because a bodily part is negated with respect to Allah the Exalted. This is like your saying: "this is the face of the matter and the command," meaning its reality and essence. Most people read "dhu al-jalal" as an attribute of the word "wajh." 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "dhi al-jalal" as an attribute of the Lord, blessed and exalted.

Allah the Exalted referred to it by a pronoun without a prior mention of it (p-170) because the meaning is clear, as He said: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], and other evidences of this kind. The indication by "perishing" applies to all existing things upon the earth, of animals and others, so the expression for those who reason prevailed, and therefore He said "man" (whoever).

"Al-wajh" (the Face) is an expression for the Essence, because a bodily part is negated with respect to Allah the Exalted. This is like your saying: "this is the face of the matter and the command," meaning its reality and essence. Most people read "dhu al-jalal" as an attribute of the word "wajh." 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "dhi al-jalal" as an attribute of the Lord, blessed and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 55, verse 19–28:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He released the two seas, meeting one another﴾ ﴿Between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿And His are the ships, sailing high on the sea like mountains﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ ﴿And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

(p-166) "Maraja al-bahrayn" means: He let them flow freely, without one being separated from the other. From it comes "marajat al-dabbah" (the animal grazed freely), and from it "al-amr al-marij," meaning a confused matter from which nothing has been distinguished. And from it (is) ﴿from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. People differed concerning "al-bahrayn." Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. Al-Hasan also said: the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea) and the Sea of Yemen and the Sea of Sham. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: a sea in the sky and a sea on the earth. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: it is the rain of the sky, which he named a sea, and the sea of the earth. The apparent meaning in my view is that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿He released the two seas﴾, intends by them the two kinds of water, the sweet and the salty; that is, He mixed them on the earth and released them intermingled in their placement on the earth, close to one another. The lesson in this interpretation is luminous. Mundhir ibn Sa'id recited:

Mixed waters, in which the sweet does not dominate the salt, pure, nor does the salt become sweet.

As for the saying of the Exalted, "yaltaqiyan" (meeting), according to the first two interpretations its meaning is: they are prepared for meeting, and it is due that they would meet were it not for the barrier. According to the third view, they meet once every year. Whoever holds that it is a sea that gathers in the sky is stating a weak view; meeting is directed in it, and in the fourth view, toward the falling of rain, and in the fifth view, toward the rivers entering the sea and the springs near the sea.

And "al-barzakh" is the barrier in everything. In some of these views it is the bodies of the earth, as Qatadah said; in some it is power. Al-barzakh also refers to the period between this world and the Hereafter for the dead, since it is a barrier. Some people said: the water of rivers does not mix with salt water, but remains in its own essence within it. This requires evidence or a sound hadith; otherwise direct observation does not necessitate it. Al-Tha'labi mentioned in "maraj al-bahrayn" enigmas and esoteric sayings to which one should not give any attention.

People differed concerning the saying of the Exalted, "la yabghiyan" (they do not transgress). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: its meaning is: neither of them transgresses against the other. Qatadah and al-Hasan also said: they do not transgress against people and inhabited places. These two views take the word from "al-baghy" (transgression). Some interpreters said: it is from your saying "baghy" when one seeks. Its meaning then is: they do not seek any state other than their two states in which they were created and subjected for them. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: "al-lu'lu'" is the large pearls and "al-marjan" is their small ones. (p-167) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, also said, as did Murrah al-Hamdani, the reverse of this. The description of smallness is the correct one for pearls. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: "al-marjan" is a red stone; this is the correct view for coral. "Al-lu'lu'" is a rare word pattern, of which no more than five are preserved in the speech of the Arabs: al-lu'lu', al-ju'ju', al-du'du', al-yu'yu' (which is a bird), and al-bu'bu', which is the original.

People differed concerning the saying of the Exalted, "minhuma" (from them). Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said in the book "al-Hujjah": some people claimed that pearls and coral do emerge from salt water and from sweet water. People refuted the poet in his saying:

He brought you whatever you wish of a lutmiyyah (a fine cloth), upon whose face the waters of the Euphrates surge.

(p-168) Most of the interpreters said: these things only emerge from the salt water in the places where rivers and sweet waters fall into it; therefore the Exalted said "minhuma." This is well known among divers. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: these things form in the sea through the falling of rain, because the oyster and others open their shells to the rain; therefore the Exalted said "minhuma." Abu 'Ubaydah said, in substance: the emergence of these things is only from the salt water, but the Exalted said "minhuma" figuratively, as the poet said:

.............. wearing a sword and a spear

And as another said:

.............. I fed them straw and cold water

(p-169) Since they are both one kind, the emergence of these things is indeed from both, even though in detail they belong specifically to one of them. This is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ [Nuh: 15] ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], whereas it is only in one of them, which is the nearest heaven to the earth. Al-Rummani said: the sweet water within them is like the pollen to the salt, so it is as one says: the child comes out of the male and the female. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the people of Madinah read "yakhruju" with a dammah on the ya' and a fathah on the ra', with "al-lu'lu'" in the nominative. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yakhraju" with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the ra', in the active form of the verb; this is also the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn al-Ju'fi from him, read "yukhriju" with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the ra', attributing it to Allah the Exalted, that is, by His enabling and power, with "al-lu'lu'" in the accusative; he also transmitted it with a nun, dammah, and a kasrah on the ra'.

"Al-jawari" is the plural of "jariyah," and it means the ships. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i read "al-jawariya" with the ya' affirmed; Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with the ya' deleted. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-munsha'at" with a fathah on the shin, meaning that Allah the Exalted or people brought them into being. Hamzah and Abu Bakr (with a variant transmitted from him) read "al-munshi'at" with a kasrah on the shin, meaning that they themselves produce the movement, advancing and retreating. "Al-a'lam" are the mountains and whatever is like them of hills and mounds. Mujahid said: whatever has a sail is among the munsha'at, and whatever has no sail raised for it is not among the munsha'at.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of the Exalted, "kal-a'lam" (like mountains), is what requires this distinction. As for the word "al-munsha'at," it includes the large and the small.

Allah the Exalted referred to it by a pronoun without a prior mention of it (p-170) because the meaning is clear, as He said: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], and other evidences of this kind. The indication by "perishing" applies to all existing things upon the earth, of animals and others, so the expression for those who reason prevailed, and therefore He said "man" (whoever).

"Al-wajh" (the Face) is an expression for the Essence, because a bodily part is negated with respect to Allah the Exalted. This is like your saying: "this is the face of the matter and the command," meaning its reality and essence. Most people read "dhu al-jalal" as an attribute of the word "wajh." 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "dhi al-jalal" as an attribute of the Lord, blessed and exalted.

[p-171] ﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him. Every day He is engaged in some affair.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two worlds (the jinn and mankind).﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through. You will not pass through except with authority.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿A flame of fire and molten brass will be sent against you, and you will have no helper.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: "يَسْألُهُ" (yas'aluhu, "asks Him"). It may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-wajh" (the Face), and the governing element in it is "yabqa" (remains), meaning: He is constantly in this state. It may also be a new independent statement, a pure report. The meaning is that every created thing, in its subsistence, its sustenance and its holding on to existence, if it is among what is provided for, is in a state of need of God, Exalted is He. As for one who asks by speech, the matter in his case is clear. As for one who is not so, his state calls for asking, so the act of asking is attributed to him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿every day He is engaged in some affair﴾ means: there appears a manifestation of His power, which preceded from eternity, at its appointed time within time, such as giving life and causing death, raising and lowering, and other matters whose end none knows but Him, Exalted and Majestic is He. "Sha'n" (affair) is a generic noun for matters. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning of the verse is the driving of decrees to their appointed times. It has been reported in some reports that God, for Him, every day in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) has three hundred and sixty glances, in which He honours and humbles, gives life and causes death, enriches and impoverishes, and other things besides. There is no god but Him. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, and it was said: 'What is this affair, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, and raises [some] and lowers [others].'" [p-171] al-Naqqash mentioned that the occasion of this verse was the saying of the Jews that God rested on the Sabbath, and so He does not carry out anything in it. Exalted is He above their saying.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two worlds﴾ is an expression for the coming of the time that was decreed and determined, when He will look into the affairs of His servants, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is not that there is some occupation from which He becomes free; rather it is a sign of threat. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Azabb al-'Aqaba: "Indeed, by God, I will certainly attend to you as long as I live." "Al-tafarrugh" (being free for something) from every human is literal. In His saying, Exalted is He, "sanafrugh" (We will attend), with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the ra', and al-A'raj and Qatada read it with a fatha on the ra' and the nun. It is related from 'Asim. It is said: "faraga" with a fatha on the ra', and "faraga" with a kasra on it; and it is valid from both together to say "yufraghu" with a fatha on the ra'. 'Isa read with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ra'. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of lower Mudar. Abu 'Amr and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with an open ya' (sayafragu, with a fatha on the ya'). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a damma on the ya'. Abu 'Amr read with a fatha on it and a damma on the ra'. Al-A'mash (according to one report) and Abu Haywa read "sayufragu" with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ra', and the verb in the passive form. 'Isa ibn 'Umar also read: "sanafrugu ilaykum" (We will attend to you).

"Al-thaqalan" (the two weights/two worlds) are the jinn and mankind. It is said of anything whose affair is great: "thaqil" (heavy), and from this is His saying: ﴿and the earth brought forth its burdens﴾ [p-172]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I am leaving among you the two weights: the Book of God and my family (ʿitra)." It is also said of ostrich eggs: "thaqal." Labid said:

"So remember a weight..."

Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said: the jinn and mankind were named "two weights" because they are heavy with sins. This is an excellent observation, looking to their creation from clay and fire. Ibn 'Amir read "ayyuhath-thaqalan" with a damma on the ha'.

People differed regarding the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾. Al-Tabari said: some people said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its estimate being: "It will be said to you: O assembly of jinn and mankind." They said: this is a report about the state of the Day of Resurrection, "the Day of Calling" (yawm al-tanad), according to the reading of the one who reads with a shadda on the dal. Al-Dahhak said: that is because people will flee to the regions of the earth, and the jinn likewise, because of what they see of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. They will find seven rows of angels surrounding the earth, so they will turn back from where they came. Then it will be said to them: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾. Some of the exegetes [p-173] said: rather, it is an address in the present world, and the meaning is: if you are able to flee from death by passing through the regions of the heavens and the earth. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: if you are able, by your minds and your thinking, to pass through and thus know the knowledge of the regions of the heavens and the earth. "Al-aqtar" (regions) are the directions. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then pass through﴾ is in the form of a command, and its meaning is incapacitation (ta'jiz). "Al-sultan" is the power over the purpose of a human being, and it is used only for the greatest of matters and for proofs, always from one who is strong in affairs. For this reason many exegetes express "sultan" as "proof" (hujja). Qatada said: "sultan" here means a king, and they have no king.

"Al-shuwaz" is the flame of fire. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and others. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: shuwaz is only from fire together with something else.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Likewise all fire is not perceived except with something else along with it.

Mujahid said: shuwaz is the green, broken-up flame. The saying of Hassan ibn Thabit, satirizing Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, supports this view:

"I satirized you, and you were humbled, an ally of disgrace, with a rhyme blazing like shuwaz."

[p-174] Al-Dahhak said: it is the smoke that comes out of the flame, and not the smoke of firewood. The majority read "shuwazun" with a damma on the shin. Ibn Kathir alone, Shibl, and 'Isa read "shiwaz" with a kasra on the shin. Both are dialects. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "nuhas" is smoke, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"It shines like the light of a lamp of sesame oil; God did not place in it nuhas."

"Al-salit" is sesame oil. The majority of reciters read "wa-nuhasun" with a raf', coordinating it with "shuwazun." Whoever says that nuhas is the well-known metal, which is the view of Mujahid and also Ibn 'Abbas, says: "molten brass will be sent against both of them," that is, it will be melted and poured on them. Whoever says it is smoke says: they will be punished with smoke sent against them. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa-nuhasin" with a jarr, coordinating it with "nar" (fire). This is correct according to what we have related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. Whoever holds that shuwaz is specific to fire estimates here: "and something of nuhas." Abu Hatim related from Mujahid that he read "wa-nihasin" with a kasra on the nun and a jarr. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra that he read "wa-nahusun" with a fatha on the nun, a damma on the ha', and a shadda on the sin, as a verb, as if he said: "and we will afflict with punishment." From Abu Jundub that he read "wa-nahsun," as you would say: "a day of nahs" (a day of misfortune). Abu 'Amr related a reading like Mujahid's from Talha ibn Musarrif, and that is a dialect for nuhas. It was also said that it is the plural of nahs. The meaning of the verse is continuous in the incapacitation of the jinn and mankind, that is: you two are in the condition of one upon whom this is sent, so you will have no helper.

There is no god but Him. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, and it was said: 'What is this affair, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, and raises [some] and lowers [others].'" [p-171] al-Naqqash mentioned that the occasion of this verse was the saying of the Jews that God rested on the Sabbath, and so He does not carry out anything in it. Exalted is He above their saying.

The meaning is not that there is some occupation from which He becomes free; rather it is a sign of threat. In His saying, Exalted is He, "sanafrugh" (We will attend), with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the ra', and al-A'raj and Qatada read it with a fatha on the ra' and the nun. It is related from 'Asim. It is said: "faraga" with a fatha on the ra', and "faraga" with a kasra on it; and it is valid from both together to say "yufraghu" with a fatha on the ra'. 'Isa read with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ra'. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of lower Mudar. Abu 'Amr and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with an open ya' (sayafragu, with a fatha on the ya'). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a damma on the ya'. Abu 'Amr read with a fatha on it and a damma on the ra'. Al-A'mash (according to one report) and Abu Haywa read "sayufragu" with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ra', and the verb in the passive form. 'Isa ibn 'Umar also read: "sanafrugu ilaykum" (We will attend to you).

"Al-thaqalan" (the two weights/two worlds) are the jinn and mankind. It is said of anything whose affair is great: "thaqil" (heavy), and from this is His saying: ﴿and the earth brought forth its burdens﴾ [p-172]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I am leaving among you the two weights: the Book of God and my family (ʿitra)." It is also said of ostrich eggs: "thaqal." Labid said:

"So remember a weight..."

Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said: the jinn and mankind were named "two weights" because they are heavy with sins. This is an excellent observation, looking to their creation from clay and fire. Ibn 'Amir read "ayyuhath-thaqalan" with a damma on the ha'.

Al-Tabari said: some people said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its estimate being: "It will be said to you: O assembly of jinn and mankind." They said: this is a report about the state of the Day of Resurrection, "the Day of Calling" (yawm al-tanad), according to the reading of the one who reads with a shadda on the dal. Al-Dahhak said: that is because people will flee to the regions of the earth, and the jinn likewise, because of what they see of the terror of the Day of Resurrection. They will find seven rows of angels surrounding the earth, so they will turn back from where they came. Then it will be said to them: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾. Some of the exegetes [p-173] said: rather, it is an address in the present world, and the meaning is: if you are able to flee from death by passing through the regions of the heavens and the earth. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Likewise all fire is not perceived except with something else along with it.

Mujahid said: shuwaz is the green, broken-up flame. The saying of Hassan ibn Thabit, satirizing Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, supports this view:

"I satirized you, and you were humbled, an ally of disgrace, with a rhyme blazing like shuwaz."

[p-174] Al-Dahhak said: it is the smoke that comes out of the flame, and not the smoke of firewood. The majority read "shuwazun" with a damma on the shin. Ibn Kathir alone, Shibl, and 'Isa read "shiwaz" with a kasra on the shin. Both are dialects. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "nuhas" is smoke, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"It shines like the light of a lamp of sesame oil; God did not place in it nuhas."

"Al-salit" is sesame oil. The majority of reciters read "wa-nuhasun" with a raf', coordinating it with "shuwazun." Whoever says that nuhas is the well-known metal, which is the view of Mujahid and also Ibn 'Abbas, says: "molten brass will be sent against both of them," that is, it will be melted and poured on them. Whoever says it is smoke says: they will be punished with smoke sent against them. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa-nuhasin" with a jarr, coordinating it with "nar" (fire). This is correct according to what we have related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. Whoever holds that shuwaz is specific to fire estimates here: "and something of nuhas." Abu Hatim related from Mujahid that he read "wa-nihasin" with a kasra on the nun and a jarr. From Abu Jundub that he read "wa-nahsun," as you would say: "a day of nahs" (a day of misfortune). Abu 'Amr related a reading like Mujahid's from Talha ibn Musarrif, and that is a dialect for nuhas. It was also said that it is the plural of nahs. The meaning of the verse is continuous in the incapacitation of the jinn and mankind, that is: you two are in the condition of one upon whom this is sent, so you will have no helper.

Every day He is engaged in some affair.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two worlds (the jinn and mankind).﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through. (p-١٧٥) His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿When the sky is split asunder and becomes red like rose-coloured oil,﴾ ﴿then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿On that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin,﴾ ﴿then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿The guilty will be recognised by their marks, and they will be seized by their forelocks and their feet,﴾ ﴿then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿This is Hell, which the guilty used to deny,﴾ ﴿they will circulate between it and scalding water, intensely hot,﴾ ﴿then which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted, and this omission is intended to convey vagueness, as if He, exalted is He, were saying: "When the sky is split asunder, how great will the terror be!" The splitting of the sky is its cleaving apart at the Resurrection. Qatadah said: "The sky is green today, but on the Day of Resurrection it will be red." So the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, "red as rose" (wardatan) is: like the redness of the rose, which is the well-known flower. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih and al-Dahhak said: it is from the colour of the rose-coloured horse, and it is feminine because the sky is feminine.

The scholars differed over His saying, exalted is He, "like oil" (kal-dihan). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it is the plural of duhn (oil). They said: on the Day of Resurrection the sky will undergo changes of colour, melting and liquefaction because of the intensity of the terror. Some said: its gleaming is likened to the gleaming of oil. A group of the interpreters (al-muta'awwilin) said: al-dihan is red leather, and the sky is likened to it. Mundhir ibn Sa'id recited:

"They sell red leather hides every evening, at the season of Badr or at the market of 'Ukaz."

His saying, exalted is He, "will not be asked" (la yus'alu) is a negation of questioning. In the Noble Qur'an there are verses which imply that there will be questioning on the Day of Resurrection, and verses which imply its negation, like this one and others. Some people said: that applies to some occasions and not others; this is the view of Qatadah and 'Ikrimah. And for the one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens. ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Both having many branches.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them are two flowing springs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them is every kind of fruit, in pairs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on couches whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens hangs low.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them are maidens restraining their gaze, whom no human or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

The "min" in His saying, Exalted is He, "And for the one who fears," may refer to all who are characterised by the fear that restrains from disobedience to Allah, Exalted is He, and it may refer to one of them. In accordance with this, some people said regarding this verse: every person who fears has two gardens. Others said: all those who fear have two gardens. The "maqam" (standing) is the servant's standing before his Lord, Exalted is He. It is explained by His saying: ﴿On the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. The standing is attributed to Allah, Exalted is He, because the servant stands before Him. Al-Tha'labi said: "maqama Rabbihi" means His standing over the servant, as evidenced by ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. Al-Zahrawi transmitted this meaning from Mujahid. In this attribution there is an indication of the difficulty of the position and an incitement to fear, which is the swiftest of the mounts to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Some people said: He meant one garden and used the dual form, as in His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf: 24], and as in the saying of al-Hajjaj: "O boy, strike his neck (two necks)." This is weak, because the sense of the dual is directed, and there is no reason to flee to this anomalous usage. The dual is supported by His saying: ﴿Both having many branches,﴾ which is the dual of "dhat," because the original form of "dhat" is "dhawat."

"Al-afnan" may be the plural of "fanan," which is the branch (ghusn). This is the view of Mujahid, and it is as though He praised the gardens for the shade and density of their branches. It may also be the plural of "fann" (kind), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both (p-178). It is as though He praised them for the abundance of the varieties of their fruit and their bounty. "Zawjan" means "two kinds." "Muttaki'in" (reclining) is a circumstantial clause (hal), either from an omitted element whose sense is: they enjoy themselves reclining, or from His saying: "And for the one who fears." "Al-ittika'" (reclining) is the posture of one who is at ease and enjoying pleasures.

The majority of readers read "furushin" with a damma on the ra'. Abu Haywa read "furshin" with a sukun on the ra'. It was narrated in a hadith that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "These linings are of brocade, so what of the outer surfaces?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "They are of light that shines." "Al-istabraq" is what is coarse and fine of silk brocade, and "al-sundus" is what is thin of it. The discussion of the word "istabraq" has already preceded. Ibn Muhaysin read "min istabraqin" as a verb, with the alif being a connecting alif.

"Al-jana" is what is picked of fruit. He described it as "near" (dani) because, as narrated in the hadith, a man can take it in any state, whether standing, sitting, or lying down, since it draws near to the one who desires it.

The pronoun in His saying: "fihinna" (in them) refers to the couches. It was said that it refers to the gardens, since the two gardens are, in meaning, gardens.

"Qasirat al-tarf" (maidens restraining their gaze) are the wide-eyed maidens (huri), who have restrained their glances to their husbands. Abu 'Amr, from al-Kisa'i alone, Talha, 'Isa, the companions of 'Ali, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "yatmithunna" with a damma on the mim. The majority of reciters read "yatmithunna" with a kasra on the mim. The meaning is: no one has deflowered them. This is because "tamth" is the blood of the vulva, so the menstrual blood is called "tamth," and the blood of deflowering is also called "tamth." When "tamth" is negated, approach to them by way of intercourse is negated. Al-Farra' said: "tamth" is only used when one has deflowered. Others said: "tamth" means he had intercourse with a virgin or with another.

The people differed concerning the meaning of His saying: "wa la jann" (nor a jinn). Mujahid said: jinn may have intercourse with the women of mankind together with their husbands when the husband does not mention Allah, Exalted is He, so this verse negates all intercourse. Hamza ibn Habib said: the jinn in Paradise have among their own kind maidens restraining their gaze, of their own species. So in this verse He negates deflowering from both human and jinn women. The wording may be hyperbolic and emphatic, as though He, Exalted is He, said: nothing has touched them. He intended complete generality, but He explicitly mentioned that which one would understand as capable of deflowering. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Tabari said: some Arabs say: "This camel has never had a pregnant female mount (tamatha habl qatt)," meaning it has not touched her. If this meaning is "no pregnancy has drawn blood from her," then it is close to the first meaning; otherwise it is a different meaning from what we have mentioned. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa la ja'n" with hamza.

In this attribution there is an indication of the difficulty of the position and an incitement to fear, which is the swiftest of the mounts to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Some people said: He meant one garden and used the dual form, as in His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf: 24], and as in the saying of al-Hajjaj: "O boy, strike his neck (two necks)." This is weak, because the sense of the dual is directed, and there is no reason to flee to this anomalous usage. The dual is supported by His saying: ﴿Both having many branches,﴾ which is the dual of "dhat," because the original form of "dhat" is "dhawat."

"Al-afnan" may be the plural of "fanan," which is the branch (ghusn). This is the view of Mujahid, and it is as though He praised the gardens for the shade and density of their branches. It may also be the plural of "fann" (kind), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both (p-178). It is as though He praised them for the abundance of the varieties of their fruit and their bounty. "Zawjan" means "two kinds." "Muttaki'in" (reclining) is a circumstantial clause (hal), either from an omitted element whose sense is: they enjoy themselves reclining, or from His saying: "And for the one who fears." "Al-ittika'" (reclining) is the posture of one who is at ease and enjoying pleasures.

The majority of readers read "furushin" with a damma on the ra'. Abu Haywa read "furshin" with a sukun on the ra'. It was narrated in a hadith that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "These linings are of brocade, so what of the outer surfaces?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "They are of light that shines." "Al-istabraq" is what is coarse and fine of silk brocade, and "al-sundus" is what is thin of it. The discussion of the word "istabraq" has already preceded. Ibn Muhaysin read "min istabraqin" as a verb, with the alif being a connecting alif.

"Al-jana" is what is picked of fruit. He described it as "near" (dani) because, as narrated in the hadith, a man can take it in any state, whether standing, sitting, or lying down, since it draws near to the one who desires it.

The pronoun in His saying: "fihinna" (in them) refers to the couches. It was said that it refers to the gardens, since the two gardens are, in meaning, gardens.

"Qasirat al-tarf" (maidens restraining their gaze) are the wide-eyed maidens (huri), who have restrained their glances to their husbands. Abu 'Amr, from al-Kisa'i alone, Talha, 'Isa, the companions of 'Ali, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "yatmithunna" with a damma on the mim. The majority of reciters read "yatmithunna" with a kasra on the mim. The meaning is: no one has deflowered them. This is because "tamth" is the blood of the vulva, so the menstrual blood is called "tamth," and the blood of deflowering is also called "tamth." When "tamth" is negated, approach to them by way of intercourse is negated. Al-Farra' said: "tamth" is only used when one has deflowered. Others said: "tamth" means he had intercourse with a virgin or with another.

The people differed concerning the meaning of His saying: "wa la jann" (nor a jinn). Mujahid said: jinn may have intercourse with the women of mankind together with their husbands when the husband does not mention Allah, Exalted is He, so this verse negates all intercourse. Hamza ibn Habib said: the jinn in Paradise have among their own kind maidens restraining their gaze, of their own species. So in this verse He negates deflowering from both human and jinn women. The wording may be hyperbolic and emphatic, as though He, Exalted is He, said: nothing has touched them. He intended complete generality, but He explicitly mentioned that which one would understand as capable of deflowering. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Tabari said: some Arabs say: "This camel has never had a pregnant female mount (tamatha habl qatt)," meaning it has not touched her. If this meaning is "no pregnancy has drawn blood from her," then it is close to the first meaning; otherwise it is a different meaning from what we have mentioned. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa la ja'n" with hamza.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 55, verse 58–69:

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿And besides these two are two gardens.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿In them are two gushing springs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾

(p-180) "Al-yaqut wa'l-marjan" (the rubies and the coral) are among the things whose beauty is outstanding and whose splendour the souls perceive. The comparison is made with them not in all their attributes, but in those respects in which these objects are compared and admired. Thus the ruby is compared in its smoothness and translucency, and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) describing a woman among the women of the people of Paradise: "He sees the marrow of her shin through the bone." The coral is compared in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this same manner of consideration, the Arabs named women after these things, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab, Marjanah Umm Sa'id, and others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ is a verse of promise and expansion for the souls of all believers, because it is general. Ibn al-Munkadir, Ibn Zayd and a group of the people of knowledge said: it applies to both the righteous and the wicked. The meaning is that the reward of one who does good through obedience is that good is done to him through bounty. Al-Naqqash narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained this verse, saying: "Is the reward of monotheism anything but Paradise?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And besides these two are two gardens.﴾ People differed concerning the meaning of "besides these two" (min dunihima). Ibn Zayd and others said: its meaning is that these two are below those two in rank and degree; the first two are the gardens of the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the latter two are the gardens of the people of the right (ashab al-yamin). Al-Rummani said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the four gardens are for one who fears the standing before his Lord, the Exalted. Al-Hasan said: the first two are for the foremost and the latter two for the followers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: "besides them" in nearness to the bestowers of blessings. These latter two, mentioned later, are superior to the first two. This is indicated by the fact that He described the two springs of these with gushing, and the latter two only with flowing; and He made these two "dark green" because of the intensity of the blessing, while the first two are described as having "branches" (dhawata afnan), though every garden has branches even if it is not dark green. Most people hold the first interpretation, but these are inferences that are not decisive. It is related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Two gardens are for the near ones (al-muqarrabun) of gold, and two gardens for the people of the right of silver, which are below the first two."

"Mudhammatan" (dark green) means: a blackness and darkness of freshness and greenness has overtaken its colour. Thus Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained it on the pulpit. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He who brought forth the pasture﴾ [al-A'la: 4] ﴿then made it dark stubble﴾ [al-A'la: 5]. "Al-nadhdhakhah" is the gushing spring whose water surges forth. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that they are gushing with all kinds of fruit, but this is weak.

Allah repeated "the palm and the pomegranate" because they are not among the fruits (in the general sense). Yunus ibn Habib and others said: He repeated them, though they are among the best of fruits, to honour them, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿And His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 55, verses 70–78:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿In them are good and beautiful [companions].﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Chaste maidens, sheltered in their pavilions.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful rich carpets.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾

"Khayrāt" is the plural of "khayrah," which means the most excellent of women. From this is the saying of the poet:

Abū Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī read "khayyirāt" with a shaddah on the kasra yā'. Abū 'Amr read it with a fatḥah on the yā'.

His saying, Most High, "maqṣūrāt," means: concealed and protected. The Arabs used to praise women for staying at home. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿ ……… ∗∗∗ and she neglects visiting them, and is excused. ﴾

He describes that her neighbours visit her while she does not visit them. It is narrated that the verse of al-A'shā was also dispraised, which is his saying:

﴿ As if her walk from her neighbour's house is the passing of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty. ﴾

So it was said in his dispraise: "This is one who roams about, goes out often, and enters often." From the praise of seclusion is the saying of Kuthayyir:

﴿ You are the one who made every short woman beloved to me, and the short women did not perceive that. ﴾

﴿ I desire short-curtained women, and I do not desire short-stepping ones; the worst of women are the bahātir (the loud, shameless ones). ﴾

Al-Ḥasan said: "maqṣūrāt fi al-khiyām" means: they do not wander about in the streets.

"Al-khiyām" are dwellings made of wood, rushes, and the various kinds of grass, and they are the tents of the nomadic Arabs. The "khiyām of Paradise" are houses of pearls. 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They are hollow pearl." Ibn Mas'ūd narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). If among the Arabs a dwelling is made of hair, it is called a bayt (house), and it is not called a khaymah (tent). From this is the saying of Jarīr:

﴿ When were the tents at Dhī Ṭulūḥ? I gave drink to the rain, O tents! ﴾

From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

﴿ Are their tents of al-markh, or of al-'ushur? ....... ﴾

He is asking: are they people of the highlands of Najd or of the lowlands? Because 'ushur does not grow except in Tihamah, and al-marakh does not grow except in Najd.

"Al-rafraf" is what hangs down from the beds of fine garments and carpets. Ibn Jubayr said: "Al-rafraf are the gardens of Paradise." The first view is more correct and clearer. The basis of Ibn Jubayr's view is that it comes from "raffa al-nabtu," when the plant became lush and beautiful. What hangs around the tent from a transparent cloth is called rafraf, and people still call it that today. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: "al-rafraf: the cushions (marāfiq)." And "al-'abqarī": fine carpets with images and other designs, made in 'Abqar, which is a place where embroidery, brocade, and the like are made. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "al-'abqarī: the zarābī (rugs)." Ibn Zayd said: "they are the ṭanāfis (cushions)." Mujāhid said: "they are thick brocade." Zuhayr al-Farqabī read "rafārif" in the plural without tanwīn (unpronounced). Abū Ṭama'ah al-Madanī and 'Āṣim, in some of what is narrated from him, read "rafārifin" with tanwīn. 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān, may Allah be pleased with him, also read "rafārifin wa 'abāqiriyyin" in the plural with tanwīn, and this was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Zajjāj and al-Rummānī erred in regarding this reading. 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān also read, in some of what is narrated from him, "'abāqariya" with a fatḥah on the qāf and the yā'. This is based on the view that the name of the place is "'abāqar" with a fatḥah on the qāf, but the correct name of the place is "'abqar." Imru' al-Qays said:

﴿ As if the clinking of the pebbles of al-Marw when it is struck is the clinking of counterfeit dinars being tested in 'Abqar. ﴾

Al-Khalīl and al-Aṣma'ī said: When the Arabs find something good and excellent, they say: "'abqarī."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have not seen among people an 'abqarī who surpasses his peers in his excellence." 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "al-'abqarī is the leader and the eye of the people." Zuhayr said:

﴿ With horses upon which is a 'abqarī garden, they deserve, one day, to attain and to rise above. ﴾

It is said: 'Abqar is a dwelling of the jinn. Dhū al-Rummah said:

﴿ Until it is as if the meadows of al-Quff are clothed by it with the embroidery of 'Abqar, a covering and a spreading. ﴾

Al-A'raj read "khuḍur" with a ḍammah on the ḍād.

The majority of people read "dhī al-jalāl" following "al-Rabb" (the Lord). Ibn 'Āmir and the people of Syria read "dhū al-jalāl" following "al-ism" (the name). Likewise in the first occurrence. In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd, may Allah be pleased with both of them, it is "dhī al-jalāl" in both places. In this verse the name is meant to refer to what it names, and supplication with these two words is good and hoped to be answered. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Persist in calling upon Him, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour."

The commentary on Surat al-Raḥmān is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
